resources.string: Written in 5/4 time and inspired by the aesthetics of Béla Bartók and Alberto Ginastera, \'Eruption\' was created by Keith Emerson on the Moog Modular synthesizer. Greg Lake first rejected the concept as too complex, but the 20-minute suite became a defining landmark of British progressive rock in 1971.

Recorded at Advision Studios in London in January 1971, produced by Greg Lake and engineered by Eddy Offord. Emerson used a Moog Modular 1C with deliberately detuned oscillators to create the \'raw\' sound of the creature Tarkus.

resources.string: Mike Oldfield was only 19 when he recorded almost every instrument at The Manor studio, layering dozens of tracks on analog tape. The album launched Richard Branson\'s Virgin Records in 1973 and reached a worldwide audience when director William Friedkin used it in the classic soundtrack of \'The Exorcist\'.
Recorded between autumn 1972 and spring 1973 at The Manor in Oxfordshire. Oldfield played guitars, bass, mandolin, Farfisa synthesizer and the famous orchestral tubular bells.

resources.string: Third movement of the \'Suite bergamasque\', inspired by Paul Verlaine\'s poem of the same name from 1869. Composed from 1890 and revised in 1905, the piece evokes moonlight through rubato tempo, subtle polyrhythm and impressionist pentatonic scales that challenged traditional German Romantic harmony.
The piece was published in 1905 by the French music publisher Eugène Fromont, after nearly 15 years of meticulous revision of the original score by the composer.

resources.string: Published in Paris in 1888, the composition broke with the virtuosity of the 19th century through soft modal cadences and static major seventh chords. It is regarded as a fundamental precursor of modern ambient music, minimalism and the idea of music for furniture (\'musique d\'ameublement\').
First published in the periodical \'Le Chat Noir\' and later as a printed score by Satie\'s father, Alfred Satie, in Paris in 1888.

resources.string: Digitally generated acoustic test signal for measuring spectral response and finding resonant nodes in the room or in the headphones. It makes it possible to assess transducer linearity at 60 Hz (sub-bass), 1 kHz (vocal reference) and 10 kHz (treble presence), without masking or dynamic compression.
Generated as linear 16-bit 44.1 kHz PCM with no dither and no dynamic range compression. Based on the AES-67 and IEC 60268-7 electroacoustic calibration standards.
